newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU ministers agree budget pact, key details open.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers agree budget pact, key details open.

text.p: European finance ministers on Friday agreed key elements of a deal to ensure sound budget policies under a single European Union currency but left crucial unresolved details to be decided by EU leaders later in the day.

After a marathon session of talks lasting nearly 11 hours and ending just before three in the morning, ministers failed to pin down the exact economic conditions which would exempt countries with excessive budget deficits from EU fines.

Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn, host of the meeting, made clear EU leaders meeting for a two-day summit starting on Friday still had to endorse a compromise proposal which fell far short of Germany's original hopes for very strict rules.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, father of the stability pact to ensure fiscal rigour under a single currency, came to Dublin seeking a deal exempting high-deficit nations from fines only if their economies shrank by over 1.5 percent in a year.
Bonn's partners argued this was too tough and the late night proposal saw nations being able to plead special circumstances as soon as their economies notched up a contraction of only 0.75 pecent.
It was still not certain whether the EU leaders would accept the principle of putting figures to these exceptional economic circumstances.
"We have an agreement on the architecture of the stability pact," French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said.
And he appeared confident that the heads of state and government would finalise the deal.
"There is nothing left which is of a nature to prevent an agreement," Arthuis said as he left the talks.
Waigel appeared less certain, emphasising that there was no full agreement yet.

Failure to clinch an accord over the next few days would upset financial markets where there is concern that disagreement over the details of a single currency might throw the whole concept into doubt.
The stability pact is a key element of a report on EMU due to be studied by EU leaders at the summit proper.

Other aspects of the report have already been informally agreed. They include the legal basis for the euro and a new post-EMU exchange rate mechanism to keep EU currencies outside the euro bloc stable.
The EU leaders were also due to discuss at the summit the bloc's long-term future, in the shape of a draft EU treaty written by the Irish EU presidency.
"What we are aspiring towards is bringing Europe closer together. We want to see a closer union of the peoples of Europe," Irish Prime Minister and summit host John Bruton said.

The Irish draft treaty shows the majority of countries are heading towards closer cooperation in crime fighting, joint employment policies, stronger foreign policy links and a true border-free Europe with common asylum and immigration policies.
It also calls on the EU to create an area of freedom, security and justice ensuring the free movement of people.

Of all the leaders coming to Dublin, British Prime Minister John Major will be among the most watched. With his ruling Conservative party torn apart over Europe, Major will be under pressure not to appear too conciliatory to his EU colleagues.
Britain opposes most of the proposals under discussion for the draft treaty -- which is supposed to prepare the bloc for enlargement into central and eastern Europe.
London also has an opt-out on the single currency, making discussions on post-EMU life something of a political minefield for the embattled British leader.
